clinicalPearls: Classically defined by a triad of agenesis of the corpus callosum, chorioretinal lacunae and infantile spasms
Almost exclusively affects females and is presumed lethal in males, consistent with an X-linked dominant disorder with sporadic de novo mutations
The pathognomonic ocular finding is multiple well-circumscribed chorioretinal lacunae clustered around the optic disc, representing depigmented defects of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid
Optic disc anomalies such as coloboma or hypoplasia frequently accompany the lacunae
Infantile spasms typically begin in the first months of life and the electroencephalogram may show a burst-suppression or split-brain pattern
Additional features include costovertebral anomalies, developmental delay and a range of other brain malformations
Diagnosis rests on the clinical triad supported by neuroimaging and dilated fundus examination, with genetic testing of limited yield
reference.pathophysiology: Aicardi syndrome is a developmental disorder attributed to a presumed X-linked dominant mutation that is lethal in hemizygous males, so surviving affected individuals are almost always female, and cases are typically sporadic and de novo. The disturbance affects early neural and neural crest development, producing agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and other cortical malformations, an epileptic encephalopathy manifesting as infantile spasms, and characteristic chorioretinal lacunae from focal maldevelopment of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid. The optic nerve is often colobomatous or hypoplastic. The combination of severe structural brain abnormality and early seizures underlies the marked neurodevelopmental impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum
Congenital toxoplasmosis or other congenital infection with chorioretinal scarring
Optic disc coloboma with retinal changes
Other causes of infantile spasms (e.g. tuberous sclerosis)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to demonstrate callosal agenesis and associated malformations
Dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging for chorioretinal lacunae and optic disc anomalies
Electroencephalography for infantile spasms and the characteristic pattern
Genetic and metabolic testing to exclude alternative diagnoses
redFlags: Onset of infantile spasms requiring prompt neurological assessment and treatment
Progressive neurological deterioration or intractable epilepsy
Signs of raised intracranial pressure from associated malformations such as cysts
Feeding difficulties and failure to thrive complicating severe disability
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with significant developmental impairment and often refractory epilepsy; survival and function vary with the severity of the brain malformation and seizure control, though the visual lacunae themselves are non-progressive.
pitfalls: Mistaking chorioretinal lacunae for the scars of congenital infection
Overlooking the diagnosis in a girl presenting with infantile spasms
Assuming a normal fundus excludes the syndrome without a dilated examination
Expecting a defined single-gene test result given the largely clinical diagnosis
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Treat infantile spasms with hormonal therapy such as corticotropin or corticosteroids, or with vigabatrin, escalating for the frequently refractory epilepsy
Combine antiseizure medications and consider the ketogenic diet or epilepsy surgery for drug-resistant seizures
Provide early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for developmental delay
Arrange ophthalmological monitoring of chorioretinal lacunae and optic disc anomalies and support visual function
Screen for and manage associated costovertebral and other anomalies with orthopaedic and paediatric input, including scoliosis as it develops
Provide nutritional and respiratory support as required
Offer genetic counselling, noting the almost exclusively female occurrence and typically sporadic de novo origin
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through paediatric neurology, ophthalmology and developmental services
